newsitem.title: POLAND: Pope takes helicopter trip over beloved mountains.
newsitem.headline: Pope takes helicopter trip over beloved mountains.

text.p: Pope John Paul toured his beloved Tatra mountains by helicopter on Thursday, midway through a sentimental journey he is using to prod Poles into exercising their new economic and political freedoms justly.
On the sixth day of his trip, the 77-year-old Polish Pope had no public engagements as he returned to the area where he loved to relax and meditate as a young man, priest and bishop.
He was billeted in a secluded Church-owned retreat in the highland resort of Zakopane, his privacy jealously guarded by Polish and Vatican security officials.
The Pope, an avid hiker and skier until 1994 when he slipped in his bath and broke his leg, was flown for more than two hours over favourite hill walks and a river where he used to canoe.
The helicopter briefly landed near a small church in the mountains so the Pope could bless a group of waiting people.

The sweeping vistas of the Tatra region are precious to the sometimes frail Pope, who appears reinvigorated by the scent and feel of his homeland and the rapturous welcome of more than a million Poles.
"The Pope was happy to revisit a series of places that are dear to him," Vatican spokesman Joaquin Navarro-Valls said. "It's very clear that he is very happy to be home."
The Pope's rest day gave both him and his fellow Poles a pause to take stock of the messages he has been hammering since arriving on Saturday for his seventh trip home.
Speaking like a concerned but stern father, he has expressed deep worry about some changes since Poland in 1989 became the first Eastern European country to cast off communism.

While the Pope has congratulated Poles on their economic achievements since then, he has warned of a moral wilderness and a get-rich-quick mentality as the once-centralised economy soars to new heights.
Realising that Poles themselves are questioning their country's direction, the Pope has pulled no punches on some of the most burning issues dividing them, chiefly abortion.
He railed against the practice on Wednesday in the central city of Kalisz, saying economically and culturally successful societies were still barbarian if they allowed it.

Whether abortion should remain liberalised or be restricted again has become a key issue in the campaign for September's elections, in which a powerful alliance centred around the pro-Catholic Solidarity union is rivalling the ruling ex-communists.
"A nation which kills its own children is a nation without a future," he told Poles in one of his most emotional remarks.
Another theme has been the fate of Poles impoverished during the country's dizzying economic development.
As in other post-communist countries, economic change has left many floundering in its wake and created a new rising class of people more adept at capitalism's rough-and-tumble rules.

The Pope warned that a new wall of economic and political selfishness had arisen in Europe and was threatening the unity of the continent just as much as the Berlin Wall did before the fall of communism.
When the Pontiff arrived in Poland last Saturday, President Aleksander Kwasniewski, an ex-communist, asked him to help build bridges and not walls between political opponents.
The Pope has responded with a series of forceful challenges to the government on social issues that may influence the political debate after he returns to the Vatican on June 10.
